title: Under the Forest Roof
objectives: I can use ten words to describe what a forest looks, sounds, and feels like.
I can use sense words to picture a place in my mind.
I can find two small words inside a compound word.
I can write a short description of a forest using words from this unit.
rationale: A single setting gives students a dense field of sight, sound, and touch words that they can use in science reading and in descriptive writing. The ten words sort into the layers and places of a forest (canopy, undergrowth, thicket, hollow), what plants look like (dense, gnarled, tangle), and sounds, wetness, and change (rustle, moist, decay). Undergrowth is also the year's first compound word, so students practice splitting a long word into two small words they already know.

passage.title: A Walk in the Woods
paras: On Saturday, Ben and his aunt hiked into an old forest. The trees grew so close together that the woods felt dense, and the air was cool and moist. High above, the leafy canopy hid the sky, so only small spots of light reached the ground.
Ben heard a rustle in the undergrowth. He froze. His aunt pointed to a thicket of bushes, and a small rabbit hopped out. "Forests are full of hiding places," she whispered.

They passed a gnarled oak whose branches twisted like old fingers. A hollow in its trunk was big enough for an owl. Ben found a tangle of vines hanging beside it and a fallen log on the ground. "That log will decay slowly," his aunt said. "It will turn into soil, and new plants will grow from it."
Ben looked at the soft, brown wood and smiled. The forest was not a gloomy place at all. It was busy and alive, even in the quiet.

A forest is full of life and hiding places.
qs.why: Ben sees animals, old trees, and decaying wood that all show a forest full of life.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words for the layers, plants, sounds, and changes in a forest. They read a short narrative that uses the words, split the compound word undergrowth into two small words, and write a description of a forest.

notes.va.dense.adj: Dense means tightly packed, and it works for fog, forests, and crowds. Have students compare two pictures, one dense and one open, and say what they could not see through.
notes.va.thicket.n: A thicket is a group of plants, not a single one. Ask students which animals use thickets and why a thicket is a good hiding place.
notes.va.rustle.v: Rustle is soft and dry. Have students make the sound with paper, then use the verb in a sentence about a quiet place.
notes.va.canopy.n: Canopy is a science word for the top layer. Draw a forest side view and label canopy, undergrowth, and ground together with the class.
notes.va.decay.v: Decay is a slow process, not a sudden event. Connect it to what the forest does with fallen leaves: nothing is wasted.
notes.va.moist.adj: Moist is between dry and wet. Use a damp paper towel to show moist, then ask students to name a moist place in the forest.
notes.va.tangle.n: Tangle is a noun here (a messy knot). Students may know it as a verb; that is fine, and the unit teaches the noun. Use string for a hands-on tangle.
notes.va.hollow.n: Hollow has two jobs. As a noun it is the empty space; as an adjective it means empty inside. Teach the noun first, then show the adjective with a hollow log.
notes.va.gnarled.adj: The g is silent, as in gnat. Ask students to draw a gnarled branch and a smooth branch side by side and label each.
notes.va.undergrowth.n: Undergrowth is a compound word: under + growth. Have students point to the two parts and say why the name fits the plants at the bottom of a forest.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The story says the trees grew close together and the sky was hidden. Dense means packed tightly, so dense fits the forest. I can picture a rustle too, because the author tells me what made the sound. I use the clues around a word to check that my meaning makes sense.'
